title: Sesshin, the last day
hookLine: stillness, and the tea at the end

lines: A KETTLE COMES DOWN THE ROW.
cards: By the last morning of sesshin, the hall sounds different. The same bells, the same wall, the same rows of cushions. But the shuffling has stopped.
Nobody shifts their weight every few minutes. The ache in the knee may still be there, but the arguing about it has gone quiet. Then the final bell rings, and it doesn't call anyone to sit again.
Someone comes down the row with a kettle. A small cup is set before each person, and tea is poured.

teach.b: First, the stillness. Some students who sit sesshin describe the later days as quieter, not because the mind has gone blank, but because it has stopped fighting the schedule. The bells ring and the body goes.

Sitting has become ordinary, and some Zen teachers say that ordinariness is closer to the point than any fireworks. Second, tea in Zen. Tea and Zen have kept company for a long time in China and Japan.
Tradition says monks drank it to stay awake through long sittings, and serving tea became a practice of its own, done with full attention.
Some sesshins end with tea served in the hall, simply, in silence, before talking begins. Third, an old Zen story.
The Chinese teacher Zhaozhou asks a newly arrived monk, have you been here before? Yes, says the monk. Go have some tea.
He asks another. No, says the second monk. Go have some tea.
The puzzled temple steward asks why he told both the same thing. Zhaozhou calls his name. The steward answers.
Go have some tea. Whatever you've done or not done, whatever you know or don't, the next thing is the cup in front of you. Fourth, the tea at the end.
After days of effort, the last teaching is a warm cup held in two hands, drunk slowly, with nothing to achieve.
No insight announced. Just tea, and then people get up, wash the cups, and go home.

how: Zen sesshin end in different ways from hall to hall; in some, tea is served to each sitter in silence before the retreat closes and talking resumes, and tea itself is prepared and drunk as a practice of attention in Zen communities.

o: a single night of sitting with no sleep at all
a several-day Zen retreat that some halls end with tea
a Japanese tea ceremony held once a year at temples

games.q: the last day of sesshin: tap the pairs.
p: asked why, and got tea too

s: a sesshin ends with the teacher announcing who has awakened
in some halls it ends quietly, with a cup of tea.
tradition says monks drank tea to stay awake through long sittings
and serving tea became a practice in its own right.
Zhaozhou gave different advice to the monk who had been there before
both got the same answer: go have some tea.

games.q: you're the temple steward. Zhaozhou just told two newcomers, one who'd been there and one who hadn't, to go have some tea. you ask him why. what does he do?
o: calls your name, and tells you to go have some tea.
games.why: he calls the steward's name, the steward answers, and Zhaozhou says: go have some tea. the answer is the cup in front of you.

practice: Hold a cup of tea, coffee or water in both hands, or hold your empty hands as if a cup were in them, and feel its warmth or coolness and its weight.
Bring it to your lips slowly and take one small sip, tasting it fully, then set it down and breathe. Nothing to figure out, nothing to finish: just this cup, and then this one.

wordCard.voice: Sesshin. A Zen retreat of several days, which, in some halls, ends not with a speech but with stillness, and a small cup of tea. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyana, meditative absorption; the name Chan in Chinese and Zen in Japanese is traced to it.

carryVoice: Your line: the tea at the end. Been here before or not: tea. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Recorded sayings of Zhaozhou (Zhaozhou Congshen), 'go have some tea'
